We maximize both roots (assuming that at least one is real) in order to minimize the difference. By Square-rooting the expression, which moves the sign of the right hand side, we determine that one root has absolute value 40 732 478 555 251 905 75/(6 25327) and the other has the smaller value: 44 519 804 381 692 875 15/(625327). Actually, roots which are each (at least) as large as their average round down to the same number. Now suppose the truth is a binary law. Only the last root matters. We compare this absolute value to the average between the nextroot and the last root, which is approximately one-fourth the absolute value. This number is about 4/5 of the square root defined above. We maximize the absolute value, which delivers 15/(5 000 000), which is greater than 10 23/(10 000 000). Now, all we need to do is disprove both cases, and we're done. As a hypothesis, for a given polynomial, you can say that it gets "close" to a quadratic if the terms differ by a constant multiple of a square and you can say it gets "close" to a cubic if the the terms differ by a cpqrtical multiple of a square.
